segments.text: Occupational English Test. Practice listening test.
This test has three parts. In each part you'll hear a number of different extracts. At the
start of each extract you'll hear this sound. You'll have time to read the questions before
you hear each extract and you'll hear each extract once only. Complete your answers as
you listen. At the end of the test you'll have two minutes to check your answers. Part
A. In this part of the test you'll hear two different extracts. In each extract a health
professional is talking to a patient. For questions 1 to 24 complete the notes with information
you here. Now, look at the notes for extract 1.
This is a benchmark education solution sample test paper. Extract 1. Questions 1-12. You
hear a pediatrician talking to a mother about her baby. Her questions 1-12 complete the
notes with a word or short phrase. You now have 30 seconds to look at the notes.
Hello, it's nice to see you, Mrs Johnson. And who do we have here?
Hi, this is Alex.
So I see that Alex is one month old, is that right?
Yes, that's right, one month.
Before we get into what may be going on with Alex, let's go through your medical history
a bit. Was your pregnancy with Alex complicated?
No, not at all. Alex was born after a full-term pregnancy with no complications or anything
like that. He weighed just under three kilos at birth. 2.94 to be exact.
Very good birth weight. And what about your family and family history of chronic disease?
Yes, let me think. Hypertension and diabetes are prevalent on both sides of the family,
but I'm not sure how far back it goes. I don't know much about my husband's grandparents.
Hmm, okay. So I understand that you have a number of concerns about little Alex, Mrs.
Johnson.
Yes, I do. Do you see how yellow Alex's eyes are? They've gotten worse over the last couple
of days. I mean, I know John dis is pretty common in newborns, but it doesn't usually
go on for this long, does it? And it isn't supposed to get worse, is it? Also, even
for a newborn, Alex has quite an irregular sleep schedule. He frequently gets his days
and nights mixed up.
Okay, well, the irregular sleep pattern is somewhat normal, but I am concerned by the
yellow colour of his eyes, particularly if it's getting worse. Neo-natal jaundice is
common and usually does not require treatment, but the presence of jaundice after the first
couple of weeks of life is worrying. I'm going to evaluate Alex for colostasis. He
He showed increased levels for bilirubin in his last visit two weeks ago, but we will
need to do further testing to assess the direct bilirubin concentration.
What is that?
Is it serious?
Colostasis is a condition in which bile cannot go from the liver to the duodenum.
This causes a waste product in the blood, bilirubin, to accumulate in the bloodstream.
It is a likely explanation for the colour of his eyes.
In terms of seriousness, that all depends on the cause of the colostasis.
The two most common causes are idiopathic neonatal hepatitis and biliary atresia.
But we will need to do more testing before we can get to a definitive diagnosis.
Okay, there is one more thing, the matter of the broken leg.
That's quite alarming.
How did that happen?
Did he fall?
No, nothing like that. I was changing his diaper and he suddenly started streaming as
I was pulling his bottom up to slide the diaper underneath. It was so frightening. I mean,
Alex is my second child and nothing like this ever happened with my first born.
Hmm, Alex's temperature, respirations and heart rate are all within normal limits, but
he does appear to be somewhat irritable. Also, hmm, his spleen and liver feeling large. I'm
I'm going to order an ultrasonography examination of the liver.
Oh my, what will happen after that?
It depends, but we might have to do a liver biopsy to further assess the damage and enlargement
of the liver and spleen.
During this time, I'm going to bring a pediatric hepatologist onto the team to help with Alex's
care.
Pediatric hepatologists are doctors that are specially trained in the diagnosis and management
of all types of childhood liver disease.
I'm still concerned about the broken leg.
It could be related to problems in the liver or a lack of vitamin D concentration.
We will need to check that as well.
Yes, it's so difficult to make him comfortable and get into sleep with the broken leg.
It causes him too much pain.
I mean, I can't imagine.
This is a Benchmark Education Solution Sample Test Paper.
You hear an occupational therapist conducting an assessment of a patient named Josh Edwards.
For questions 13-24, complete the note with a word or short phrase.
You now have 30 seconds to look at the notes.
Hello. It is Mr Edward's correct?
Yes, yes, that's correct, but you can call me Josh.
Okay, Josh. We are here today for me to conduct an occupational therapy assessment to review
the equipment needs in your home to support you in managing transfers more independently.
How does that sound?
That sounds great.
Let's first take a look at your accident. I see here that you were involved in a traffic
accident about five months ago.
Yes, and it was quite a serious one. I sustained significant injuries to my left leg, particularly
my ankle. Yes, quite serious John. You have already undergone several reconstructive surgeries.
Is that correct? Yes, that is quite correct. I've been through a few surgeries already,
but I'm still waiting on further surgery, which they tell me will be done in the next
few months. So you are still non-weight bearing on your left leg, and I see you are still
using clutches provided by the hospital. I guess you could put it that way. It has
been quite a struggle managing the crutches. Also because of the significant swelling in
my left ankle, I've been advised to keep my leg elevated much of the day. So, in general,
not a lot of moving around for me.
Hmm, I see. So, as I said, John, I'm here to data review the equipment needs to help
support you in managing transfers. You currently need physical assistance to get on and off
the bed as well as chairs. Is that right?
Yes, that's right. I'm constantly having to bother my wife or teenage son to help me.
I hate being such a bother. So sometimes I end up staying in bed for much of the day,
you know, to keep out of the way. I mean, I do sometimes ask my son to help me sit on
the couch.
How is that for you? Any pain while sitting on the couch?
No, not while sitting on the couch, but as the sofa is low, my son has to pull me to
standing before I can use my crutches. I often experience spinal and neck pain after sitting
on the sofa, and I think him pulling me is part of the reason why. Also, when I sit on
the couch, I have to sit along the length of the couch, so my neck is always twisted if
I try to watch the TV or talk with anyone.
Hmm, I think we can definitely help with that. I'm going to recommend a more suitable chair
that I think would be of significant benefit.
The chair has a rise function that will enable you
to manage an independent sit to stand transfer,
which will reduce your dependency on your family,
as well as the risk of injury from the technique
you are currently using to stand up from the couch.
Sounds interesting.
What about my legs?
How will I keep them elevated?
The chair also has a leg rest elevation function,
so it will help you to sit in an aligned position
with your legs elevated. This will help you to reduce the twisted neck you spoke about.
We can put the chair anywhere you would like, but I think it would be a good idea to put
it here in the main lounge. To reduce your isolation and the amount of time you spend
in the bedroom, how does that sound? That sounds fantastic. So what do we do next? How
do I go about getting this chair? We will set up a joint visit to a local seating provider
who can offer you a variety of options to maximise choice and value.
We will make sure that you get a chair that meets your clinical needs
as well as your choices regarding fabrics and colours.
I mean the chair will be in your main lounge for at least a few months if not more.
Yes that will make my wife happy.
That is the end of part A. Now, look at part B.
B. For questions 25 to 30, choose the answer A, B or C, which fits best according to what
you hear. You'll have time to read each question before you listen. Complete your answers
as you listen. Now look at question 25. You hear a morning briefing on a ward. Now read
the question.
Hello all, so let's get started. Felicity, can you start off this morning's briefing?
Yes, I certainly can. So first up we have a 99 year old woman with a history of high
blood pressure, congestive heart failure and knee osteoarthritis. She is presenting
with abdominal pain, increasing over five days, along with obstipation in the last day.
Exam showed abdominal distention, hypoactive bowel sound and no mass found.
Okay, so next steps.
Based on a symptoms and physical exam, an abdominal CT scan and volume,
Repletion are the next steps.
Question 26.
You hear a trainee nurse asking a mentor for advice.
Now read the question.
Hello Jane, I have a patient I would like to discuss with you.
Sure, tell me what you have.
I have a 32 month old boy who was brought to the outpatient pediatric clinic because of
weakness and failure to thrive.
He is 3 kilograms below the expected weight for his age and physical examination revealed
a febrile fussy child who does not like to be touched.
According to his mother, he doesn't have diarrhea but his appetite is poor.
I mean, I know where the evidence is pointing me but...
What working differential diagnosis are you considering for the child?
Hmm, the mother and the child have never been tested for HIV, so that is a possibility,
along with TB, malnutrition from lack of food, enteric parasitic infections or combinations
of these etiologies.
I agree with you.
So what is your next course of action?
Question 27. You hear a nurse talking to another nurse about the discharge of a patient.
Now read the question.
Hmm, Jack, can I speak to you for a moment?
Yes, what's on your mind?
I noticed you seem to be a bit hostile towards the HIV infected mother who is about to be
discharged with her baby boy.
You should be focused on teaching your patients some important counselling messages before
she leaves, but instead it seems to be difficult for you to have a conversation with her.
I know, but I just can't stop thinking that women like her should never have children.
She put her poor infant in possible danger because of her foolishness.
Remember, we are here to protect our patients' rights, not judge them for past choices.
Also, think about how you would feel if you were in the patient's shoes or had a close
relative with HIV. Would you want them to be discriminated against?
Question 28. You hear a nurse talking about a new education
program for parents. Now read the question.
Hello everyone. Today, Kathy from the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit is going to talk about
a new education program for parents that is being developed.
Thank you for allowing me to talk about this new program.
What we are aiming to do is develop a teaching plan for parents of premature babies who are
nearly ready for discharge.
We have to take into account that these infants might have any number of physical needs upon
discharge, including special feeding instructions, apnea monitors, temperature instability among
others and that the parents will be anxious, tired and possibly in pain in the case of
post-susarion mothers. I am here to get your feedback on three priority areas we have identified.
Risk for abnormal body temperature fluctuations, risk for ineffective breathing patterns and...
In question 29, you hear a doctor in the A&E discussing a case with a nurse.
Now read the question.
Any luck getting Mr Walker to agree to contact his daughter?
No, Dr Avery. He insists on not bothering her at her job, but he doesn't seem to know
anything about his condition. He told me he takes a blue pill for his high blood in the
morning and two pink pills at dinner. I mean, he nodded when I explained to him that he
should elevate his left foot and apply ice packs, but…
Who knows if he actually understood you, or if he will tell his daughter what happened.
Do you think that the friend that followed the ambulance here will be any help?
Hmm, no, I don't think so. I mean she seems welly and able to get him home, but she also has no idea of what medication she's on.
I really think we should wait to see if we can contact the daughter.
Question 30. You hear a hospice nurse explaining intake protocol for new patients. Now read the question.
Over the next 48 hours, I will have a series of meetings with you to explain the options
and assist in decision-making choices for your loved ones.
Other team members include the hospital palliative care team, the nursing staff, the physician,
chaplain and the social worker, all of whom will also take part in these meetings.
The first meeting will cover prognosis, code status and treatment options and the second
meeting will cover nutrition, hydration and treatment of any concurrent illnesses.
Then, we will have a meeting discussing palliative care and hospice as well as the scope of available
resources.
The fourth and final meeting will introduce the concept of de-escalating care, initiation
of comfort measures and the involvement of family and friends.
You will have the opportunity to ask questions at each session.
And we will also...
That is the end of part B.
Now look at part C.
Part C. In this part of the test, you'll hear two different extracts. In each extract, you'll
hear health professionals talking about aspects of their work.
For questions 31 to 42, choose the answer A, B or C, which fits best according to what
you hear. Complete your answers as you listen.
Now look at Extract 1.
Extract 1.
Questions 31-36.
You hear an interview about a career development in occupational therapy.
You now have 90 seconds to read questions 31-36.
This is a benchmark education solution sample test paper.
[Unclear interval — replay the original audio.]
Hello Mrs Craig.
This is Craig is an honorary fellow at Bridgmont University and is a regular contributor to
the official journal of the College of Occupational Therapists.
We are pleased to have you here today to talk about career development in occupational therapy.
So please start off by giving us a little bit of history about the topic.
Yes, thank you James for the introduction.
I am very happy to be here to talk about a topic that is near and dear to my heart.
Until about a decade ago, occupational therapists in the United Kingdom were fortunate in that
demand for therapists exceeded supply.
There was little need to think of career development since posts and promotion aspects were plentiful.
I understand that you are implying that the situation has changed over the years.
Is that correct?
Yes, and that's quite correct.
Today, occupational therapists face the same challenges
in finding a first post and developing their careers
as others do.
Fortunately, many of the attributes that make
for effective practitioners in the fields
of occupational therapy are also valuable
in professional development, in particular flexibility,
creativity, problem solving, and lateral thinking.
What have occupational therapists done with these areas of strength?
Occupational therapists have combined these strengths with entrepreneurial
ship to move to profession beyond familiar areas such as the National
Health Service and Social Services. We're starting to see therapists work in a
much wider variety of posts.
Mmm, quite interesting. What role has the College of Occupational Therapists taken to
encourage this development.
The College of Occupational Therapists has lobbied quite a bit for a change in how occupational
therapists are educated. As a result, universities have started to prepare graduates for the
future through providing role-emerging placements as well as including courses on entrepreneurial
ship in the standard curriculum. There is evidence that this change in the curriculum
encouraged new and developing areas of practice in the field, such as low vision and driving.
This is a wonderful development because just as our profession has become more diverse in the UK,
employment patterns and career paths have become less predictable,
which means therapists need to be prepared to be more proactive and flexible in developing their own career paths.
What exactly do you mean by flexibility?
I mean that graduates seeking a first post need to be willing to start where opportunities
occur and to work to create a path towards their ultimate goal instead of holding out
for that perfect opportunity.
A short term post in occupational therapy or a related area can provide both experience
and an employment reference.
This can be combined with postgraduate study to widen knowledge in a preferred area and
enhance employability.
In addition, working in the voluntary or private sector provides a different perspective that
can be applied to work in the public sector.
In the end, each therapist has to make choices that will move him or her in the direction
of the next career goal and also be open to discover new areas in the field not previously
considered.
What kind of career path do occupational therapists with a bit of experience tend to
pursue?
experience is gained most therapists pursue a clinical career. But other avenues also exist,
for example in management, education, private practice and research. There are now more opportunities
to combine roles in lecture, practitioner or clinical researcher posts and to pursue private
practice on a part-time basis. It is becoming more and more common for therapists to work for
different employers and to move between the public, private and voluntary sectors.
So what role does continuing professional development play in the career of a therapist?
Well, continuing professional development is at the heart of an occupational therapy
career. It is the link between a current post and future aspirations and it can help to
maintain a focus on the profession while in a non-occupational therapy post. Professional
development along with active participation in the Professional Association and keeping
up to date by reading research journals can be a lifeline in an uncertain future.
So I see we have a number of people with questions. We will now give the audience the chance to.
Now look at Extract 2.
Extract 2.
Questions 37-42.
You hear a radiologist talk about the latest trends in her field.
This is a benchmark education solution sample test paper.
You now have 90 seconds to read questions 37-42.
[Unclear interval — replay the original audio.]
Thank you for the warm welcome. My name is Dr Kelly Preston and I am here today to talk
about the latest trends in the field of radiology. As we all know, for the past few years, information
technology and digital solutions have exploded in the field of radiology. It's such a hot
topic that the Radiological Society of North America recently announced that the focus
of their next annual conference will be exclusively imaging information technology solutions and
will not include other devices as in previous years.
This pivot to technology and radiology is mostly driven by the current landscape. There
is a massive demand for always on and mobile-friendly solutions in all areas of our lives, even
in the medical field. This may seem like a drawback of technology, but the medical field
will need to figure out ways to take advantage of this reality.
driver is the fast pace of innovation and advancement of available technologies. In
just a few years, machine learning and artificial intelligence have made it
possible to automate nearly anything in our lives from driving to radiological
procedures. The first trend that I'm going to expand on is in fact artificial
intelligence. Two years ago AI started to show up in demonstrations wowing all
of us. But it was last year when AI's real world impact became evident, when machine
learning solutions for detecting biomarkers in stroke patients became a reality. Experts
are also predicting that AI will lead to improvements in image acquisition by hastening MRI imaging
time, enhancing CT resolution and enabling dose reduction with PET slash CT. Another
particularly exciting development that AI technology could bring is a move toward a greater ability
to identify changes over time in imaging studies. This advancement could be particularly helpful
in mammography studies, where AI can recognise disease progression early, resulting in better
outcomes for patients. AI is a trend that will definitely continue to have an impact
on the future of radiology.
Another example of technology making its mark is big data.
Massive databases of information have been collected over the years and now machines,
more specifically machine learning, are pouring over it, processing it, organising it and
most importantly, analysing it to find relevant insights.
These deep learning solutions are being used to improve existing operations, treatments
and to discover new opportunities.
For example, huge collections of data combined with a machine learning system can help identify
better and more accurate ways to diagnose patients.
Now for a trend that doesn't involve technology.
Radiologists are more necessary than ever.
Yes, I said it.
We are more necessary than ever, despite the worries that we may have about AI and machines
replacing us.
With some of the workloads being automated by technology, radiologists are needed for
clinical care and patient interactions.
Each radiologist should serve as a point of contact for patients, allowing for better and
more down to earth explanations of various situations, treatments and actions that other
providers may not be able to provide. In fact, radiologists will become an integral part of a care
team as patients continue to push for more personalised time with their providers, which may require
radiologists to reimagine imaging workflows that aren't compatible with offering more face-time
patients. It will take time to make these changes but they will be beneficial for our patients
and the future of the field of radiology. Another technology-free trend is the growth of
interventional radiology and its divergence from diagnostic radiology. As these two specialties
continue to diverge, we will have to continue to develop different residency curricula, different
clinic emphasis and procedural work will be done less and less by diagnostic radiologists.
For many years, techniques of interventional radiology were only used to make cardiovascular
procedures less invasive, but in recent years these techniques are being used in neurology,
gastroenterology and urology. Last but not least in this list of trends are the challenges that
the field of radiology faces. One of the biggest stumbling blocks that radiologists continue to face
is convincing referring clinicians that we, the radiologists, are the experts with imaging and
should be able to communicate directly with patients about the results of imaging.
It is often difficult for referring physicians to seed control to other specialists like radiologists.
Let's hope that the trend for next year include increased communication with patients.
That is the end of part C. You now have two minutes to check your answers.
[Unclear interval — replay the original audio.]
That is the end of the listening test.
